title: Draft: Share the Go build and test cache through gobuildcache
description:
## What does this MR do?

Shares the Go build and test cache between all CI jobs through a bucket, using [gobuildcache](https://github.com/saracen/gobuildcache) as `GOCACHEPROG`, and makes test results reusable across pipelines.

Supersedes https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab-runner/-/merge_requests/5312.

1. **Stable file modification times.** `ci/touch_git_hash` sets each tracked file's mtime from its blob ID. Go's test cache records the mtime of every file a test opens, and commit dates change between pipelines: shallow clones date untouched files to the oldest fetched commit, and merged results pipelines get a new merge commit every time (https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitaly/-/issues/6614).
2. **Shared cache.** `ci/gobuildcache` sets `GOCACHEPROG` for jobs using `.go-cache`:
   - **Protected refs write.** Their job's ID token is exchanged through GCP Workload Identity Federation, which only accepts tokens for protected refs of runner projects. No key is stored anywhere.
   - **Everything else reads anonymously** (`-readonly`), including merge requests from forks, and keeps new entries local.
   - **Writers refresh the entries they use,** so the bucket's age-based lifecycle rule only expires entries nothing uses.
3. **Cacheable test runs.** Linux jobs that test `./...` use splitic's `-group-by-package`, which tests each package in its own `go test` without a `-run` pattern. Today every package's cached result is keyed on the whole bucket's `-run` pattern, and with `-coverpkg`, on every covered package in the same invocation, so almost nothing is reused.

4. **No more GitLab Go cache in these jobs.** Go doesn't use `GOCACHE` when `GOCACHEPROG` is set, so it was being restored and saved for nothing. In `binaries` on `main` it's 10 GB: 3m43s to restore and 6m54s to save, about 10 of the job's 15 minutes, against 2m28s of actual building. Windows jobs keep theirs.

## Why was this MR needed?

Measured locally on `./helpers/...` (50 test packages) with a shared bucket and a fresh local cache per run, after a one-line change to `helpers/url`: 7/50 test results cached with today's splitic, 48/50 with `-group-by-package`.

## Security

- **Writes** only come from protected refs, and GCP enforces that from the signed ID token. A pipeline for a fork's merge request run in this project can't write, even if it changes the CI config.
- **Reads** are public. Test output from protected refs ends up in the bucket, and unlike job logs it isn't masked. Tests only see the variables in `scripts/envs/allowlist_*.env`, and `scripts/envs/README.md` now says nothing secret belongs there. The only credential on those lists is `OUTER_CI_JOB_TOKEN`, which expires with the job. `GOBUILDCACHE_CREDENTIALS` is the path to a credentials config, which isn't secret; on protected refs the config points at a file holding the job's ID token, which merged test code could read.
- **Release jobs** (`* docker images`) extend `.go-cache`, so on protected refs they read and write the bucket too.

## Depends on

- https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/ci-cd/runner-tools/splitic/-/merge_requests/5 (`SPLITIC_VERSION` pins its branch)
- gobuildcache's refresh branch, https://github.com/saracen/gobuildcache/tree/ajwalker/refresh (`GOBUILDCACHE_VERSION` pins it)
- The Workload Identity Federation pool and provider in `group-verify-df9383`. Until they exist, protected refs fail to write and carry on with their local cache.

## Not included

- Windows jobs still use the GitLab cache.
- Removing the old `GOBUILDCACHE` and `GOCACHEBUILD_CREDENTIALS` project variables, and the key they held, once this works.
- Moving to a shared CI component (`gitlab-org/ci-cd/runner-tools/gobuildcache`) for use by other runner projects.

## What's the best way to test this MR?

- **MR pipelines** read the bucket anonymously, and their `-stats` lines in the job logs show hits and misses per `go` command.
- **Writes** need a protected ref, which is being tested in a separate test project.

title: Remove service health check container when the job is cancelled
description:
## What does this MR do?

Removes the service health check container (`<service>-wait-for-service`) with a context detached from the job's cancellation, bounded by `dockerCleanupTimeout`, the same way `Cleanup()` does.

## Why was this MR needed?

`runServiceHealthCheckContainer` removes the health check container in a deferred call using `e.Context`. When a job is cancelled or times out while the runner is waiting for a service, that context is already done: `ContainerRemove` fails and the error is discarded. The container is not tracked in `e.temporary`, so `Cleanup()` does not remove it either.

As a result, cancelled jobs leak health check containers on the runner host. If the health check had not finished yet, the leaked container keeps running indefinitely, polling a service that no longer exists. On our hosts we found 3 running and 28 exited leaked containers, the oldest two months old.

## What's the best way to test this MR?

- New unit test `TestRunServiceHealthCheckContainer_RemovesContainerWhenJobIsCancelled`: the waiter mock cancels the job context and returns `context.Canceled`. The test asserts that `NetworkList` and `ContainerRemove` are called with a context that is not cancelled. Without the fix, the test fails with an unexpected `ContainerRemove` call made with the cancelled context.
- `go test ./executors/docker/` passes (unit tests; integration tests skipped without Docker in the test container). `gofmt` and `go vet` are clean.
- Manual check: run a job with a slow service (for example Elasticsearch), cancel it during "Waiting for services to be up and running", then run `docker ps -a --filter label=com.gitlab.gitlab-runner.type=wait`. Before this change a container is left behind; with it, none is.

## What are the relevant issue numbers?

Closes https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab-runner/-/issues/39937
